claims.text: The world's population grew slowly for most of history, then began rising steeply from around 1750; it passed 2 billion in about 1927, 6 billion in 1999 and reached about 8 billion in 2022.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The rapid increase from about 1750 happened because death rates fell faster than birth rates: cleaner water, better sanitation, vaccines and more reliable food supplies cut deaths, while birth rates stayed high for a time.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In a country at an early stage of development both birth rates and death rates are high and the population changes little; when health care and food improve, the death rate falls first, so the gap between births and deaths widens and the population grows rapidly.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A fall in population in a wealthier country is driven by birth rates below the death rate and an ageing population, not by famine, poor sanitation or disease.

claims.text: Over-population is a relationship between people and resources, not a count of people: it means too many people for the resources and technology of an area to support a good standard of living, while under-population means too few people to use an area's resources fully.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Over-population is defined relative to resources and technology, so a country with a large population is not over-populated merely because it has many people, and a country with few people can be over-populated if it lacks the resources to feed them.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An area is over-populated when the number of people strains resources and services, so the land cannot feed everyone and housing, schools and hospitals become overloaded; an area is under-populated when there are too few people to work the land, staff services or make markets worthwhile, so resources are wasted.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The resources of an area alone do not settle whether it is over- or under-populated; the technology, investment and government of the place decide how far those resources can support the people.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Population size changes through natural causes, births and deaths, and through migration, people moving into or out of an area.

claims.text: The natural increase of a population is the birth rate minus the death rate, per 1000 people per year, and it is negative when deaths outnumber births.

claims.text: Birth rates tend to be high where many children die young, where children work on the family holding, and where few women are in paid work or education; birth rates tend to be low where family planning is widely available and where educating children is expensive.

claims.text: Death rates fall where clean water, sanitation, health care and a reliable food supply reach the people, and rise during famine, epidemic disease and war.

claims.text: Birth rate is the number of live births per 1000 people in a year, and death rate is the number of deaths per 1000 people in a year.

claims.text: The rate of natural population change differs between countries mainly because the falls in birth and death rates happen at different times: in many low-income countries the death rate has fallen with vaccination and clean water while the birth rate has stayed high, whereas in higher-income countries both rates are low, so the natural change is small or negative.

claims.text: Natural increase is birth rate minus death rate, a difference measured per 1000 people per year; net migration is a separate cause of change, immigrants minus emigrants, and population change is the two added together.

claims.text: Anti-natalist policies aim to reduce the birth rate, through family planning services, education for women, taxes or penalties for large families, and legal limits on the number of children; pro-natalist policies aim to raise the birth rate, through paid parental leave, child payments and better housing for families.

claims.text: A population policy has two sides to describe: the measures it takes, such as clinics or child payments, and the impacts it achieves, such as a lower birth rate or a smaller school-age cohort.

claims.text: China's one-child policy, in force from 1979 to 2015, used fines, workplace pressure and permits to cut the birth rate sharply, but it also left an ageing population, a shortage of workers and millions more boys than girls by the 2010s.
